questions.prompt: Why is the volatile keyword needed in embedded C?

options.text: It stops the compiler caching a value that hardware can change
It makes access to the variable atomic
It marks the variable as constant
It places the variable in flash memory

questions.explanation: Without volatile the compiler may keep a register copy and never re-read the address, so a hardware register or ISR-updated flag appears never to change.

questions.prompt: What should be avoided inside an interrupt service routine?

options.text: Clearing the interrupt source
Setting a flag variable
Reading a hardware register
Blocking calls and long processing

questions.explanation: An ISR runs with interrupts disabled or at high priority, so anything slow delays everything else. The pattern is to set a flag or queue data and return immediately.

questions.prompt: Why is dynamic memory allocation often avoided in embedded systems?

options.text: Allocation requires an operating system
malloc is not available in C
The heap is always slower than flash
Fragmentation and non-deterministic timing can cause late failures

questions.explanation: On a device with kilobytes of RAM, fragmentation can make an allocation fail after days of uptime, and allocation time is not bounded. Static or pool allocation is predictable.

questions.prompt: What is switch bounce and how is it usually handled?

options.text: Rapid make-break transitions, fixed by debouncing in software or hardware
A signal reflecting off an unterminated line
Electrical noise on power rails, fixed with a capacitor only
A switch failing permanently, fixed by replacement

questions.explanation: Mechanical contacts chatter for milliseconds, so one press reads as many. Debouncing ignores transitions within a short window, in code or with an RC filter.

questions.prompt: Which protocol uses a single data line plus a clock and supports multiple devices by address?

options.text: I2C
UART
SPI
CAN

questions.explanation: I2C uses SDA and SCL with 7-bit addressing, so many devices share two wires. SPI is faster but needs a chip-select line per device.

questions.prompt: What does a watchdog timer do?

options.text: Wakes the device from sleep on a schedule
Measures how long each task runs
Resets the system if the software stops servicing it
Logs errors to external storage

questions.explanation: Firmware must periodically kick the watchdog. If it hangs, the timer expires and forces a reset, which is how unattended devices recover from a lockup.

questions.prompt: In an RTOS, what does priority inversion mean?

options.text: The scheduler ignores priorities entirely
Task priorities are assigned in reverse order by mistake
Interrupts preempt all tasks regardless of priority
A high-priority task waits on a resource held by a lower-priority one

questions.explanation: The high-priority task is blocked, and a medium-priority task can preempt the holder so it never releases. Priority inheritance raises the holder's priority to break it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a hard and a soft real-time system?

options.text: Hard real-time is faster in absolute terms
Missing a deadline is a failure in hard real-time; degraded quality in soft
Soft real-time has no deadlines at all
Hard real-time runs on bare metal; soft uses an RTOS

questions.explanation: An airbag controller missing its deadline is a failure regardless of average speed. A media player dropping a frame is merely worse. Determinism matters more than raw speed.

questions.prompt: Why is a circular buffer commonly used for UART receive data?

options.text: It compresses the incoming data
It guarantees no data is ever lost
It decouples the ISR producer from the slower consumer without allocation
It automatically parses protocol frames

questions.explanation: The ISR writes at the head and the main loop reads from the tail, in fixed memory with no shifting. It still overruns if the consumer falls too far behind.

questions.prompt: What does a pull-up resistor on a GPIO input do?

options.text: Increases the output current the pin can supply
Converts the pin to an analogue input
Protects the pin from over-voltage
Defines a known high level when nothing is driving the pin

questions.explanation: A floating input picks up noise and reads randomly. A pull-up holds it high until a switch pulls it to ground, which is the standard button arrangement.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of using DMA for a data transfer?

options.text: It guarantees no transmission errors
It increases the bus clock frequency
It reduces the amount of RAM required
It moves data without the CPU copying each byte

questions.explanation: The DMA controller moves data between peripheral and memory independently, freeing the CPU for other work or sleep. Buffers must not be touched mid-transfer.

questions.prompt: How does PWM control the brightness of an LED?

options.text: By changing the LED's forward current continuously
By switching fast and varying the proportion of on time
By varying the supply voltage smoothly
By changing the frequency of the signal only

questions.explanation: The LED is switched fully on and off faster than the eye resolves, so average power tracks the duty cycle. Frequency only needs to be high enough to avoid visible flicker.

questions.prompt: What does sizeof(int) depend on in embedded C?

options.text: It is always 4 bytes by the C standard
The amount of RAM available
The compiler and target architecture
It is always 2 bytes on microcontrollers

questions.explanation: The standard only sets a minimum range, so int is 16 bits on some MCUs and 32 on others. Fixed-width types like uint32_t are used precisely to remove the ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Why is a struct sometimes larger than the sum of its members?

options.text: The compiler stores type information alongside it
Padding is inserted to satisfy alignment requirements
Each member gets a hidden length prefix
Structs always reserve a fixed minimum size

questions.explanation: Members are aligned to natural boundaries, so a char before an int leaves a gap. Ordering members largest-first reduces padding, which matters when memory is tiny.

questions.prompt: What is the primary technique for reducing power in a battery-powered device?

options.text: Sleeping between events and waking on interrupt
Running the CPU at maximum clock to finish sooner only
Disabling all interrupts
Using a larger flash memory

questions.explanation: Most devices are idle most of the time, and sleep current is orders of magnitude below active. Polling in a busy loop is what destroys battery life.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of sharing a variable between an ISR and main code without protection?

options.text: The interrupt is silently disabled
The variable is placed in the wrong memory section
A multi-byte value can be read while half-updated
The compiler refuses to build

questions.explanation: On an 8-bit MCU a 32-bit counter is updated in several instructions, so an interrupt mid-update yields a torn value. A critical section or an atomic type is required.

questions.prompt: What does MQTT's publish-subscribe model give an IoT deployment?

options.text: Decoupling of producers and consumers via a broker
Guaranteed sub-millisecond latency
Direct device-to-device connections without a server
Built-in encryption without TLS

questions.explanation: Devices publish to topics without knowing subscribers, so consumers can be added without touching firmware. The broker becomes a dependency and a bottleneck to plan for.

questions.prompt: Why is a firmware update mechanism usually designed with a fallback image?

options.text: To allow two features to run at once
To reduce the size of each update
To let the device recover if the new image fails to boot
To store user data during the update

questions.explanation: A power loss or a bad image mid-update would otherwise brick a device that may be physically unreachable. A/B partitions let the bootloader revert.

questions.prompt: What does an ADC's resolution of 12 bits mean?

options.text: It maps the input range onto 4096 discrete levels
Its reference voltage is 12 volts
It samples 12 times per second
It has 12 input channels

questions.explanation: Twelve bits give 2^12 steps across the reference range, so a 3.3 V reference resolves about 0.8 mV. Resolution is separate from accuracy and sampling rate.

questions.prompt: How do you typically debug firmware on a device with no console?

options.text: Waiting for the watchdog to report the fault
Recompiling with optimisation disabled only
Adding print statements to the source and hoping
A hardware debugger with breakpoints, plus toggling a GPIO to time code

questions.explanation: JTAG or SWD gives real breakpoints and memory inspection, and toggling a pin lets an oscilloscope measure timing without disturbing it the way logging would.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between flash and RAM on a microcontroller?

options.text: RAM stores the program; flash holds variables
Flash holds code and persists without power; RAM is volatile working memory
Flash is faster to write than RAM
They are the same memory with different addresses

questions.explanation: Flash is non-volatile, larger and slow to write with limited erase cycles. RAM is fast and volatile, and is usually the scarcer of the two.

questions.prompt: Why is a stack overflow particularly dangerous on a microcontroller?

options.text: It always halts the CPU immediately
It silently corrupts adjacent memory with no MMU to catch it
It erases the flash contents
It triggers an automatic firmware update

questions.explanation: Without memory protection the stack grows into globals or the heap and corrupts them, so the crash appears somewhere unrelated much later.

questions.prompt: What does a bootloader do?

options.text: Supplies power to peripherals at startup
Manages task scheduling at runtime
Runs first and starts or updates the application image
Compiles the firmware on the device

questions.explanation: It initialises the minimum hardware, decides whether to enter update mode, and jumps to the application. It is what makes field updates possible without a programmer.

questions.prompt: Why should an IoT device authenticate the server it connects to?

options.text: Because the protocol requires it for compression
To prevent a spoofed server issuing commands or malicious firmware
To reduce bandwidth usage
To synchronise its clock accurately

questions.explanation: One-way authentication leaves the device trusting whatever answers, which is how a fleet gets hijacked. Certificate validation on the device is the defence.

questions.prompt: What does the const keyword on a pointer parameter such as const char *p indicate?

options.text: The pointer itself cannot be reassigned
The parameter is passed by value
The data pointed to must not be modified
The pointer is stored in flash

questions.explanation: const char *p protects the pointed-to data; char *const p would fix the pointer instead. Reading the declaration right to left resolves the ambiguity.
